title: PH: China has no right, moral basis to dictate whom we will cooperate with
summary: China has neither the right nor moral basis to dictate how and with whom the Philippines will cooperate to defend its sovereignty and national interests, the Department of National Defense said…

blocks.text: China has neither the right nor moral basis to dictate how and with whom the Philippines will cooperate to defend its sovereignty and national interests, the Department of National Defense said Friday.

DND spokesperson Assistant Secretary Arsenio Andolong issued the statement after China's defense ministry spokesperson Chen Xi called out Japan and Australia for having defense agreements with the Philippines.
"We do not need Beijing’s permission regarding our relations with other nations, especially on matters of our defense and security," Andolong said.

"China's deceptive accusations against other countries of escalating tensions have gone too far, while it continues to use coercion, intimidation, and force to assert its illegal claims in the West Philippine Sea and other waters," he added.

The Defense official said if China truly desires peace and stability in the region, it must cease its intimidation and respect the maritime rights of other nations in accordance with international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
In a press briefing Thursday, Chen urged Japan to stop "stirring up trouble" over the South China Sea.

Chen was responding to questions over announcements earlier this month that Japan will provide the Philippines with radars and drones to boost its coastal surveillance capabilities in the latest sign of deepening defense ties between Manila and Tokyo, both formal U.S. military allies.

China also denounced a defense pact between Australia and the Philippines, arguing it would "exacerbate tensions" in a region crisscrossed by competing territorial claims and vowing to "safeguard" its rights.
The agreement between Canberra and Manila, struck this month during a visit to the Philippine capital by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, updates a decades-old memorandum.
The countries have steadily increased defense cooperation in recent years, including joint maritime patrols in the strategically vital South China Sea.

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis. US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the waterway.

"Certain Philippine politicians, driven by their selfish interests, are spreading false narratives about China, constantly engaging in provocations and stirring up trouble," Chen told a news conference on Thursday when asked about the deal.
Those individuals are "attempting to enlist the backing of forces from outside the region to embolden themselves and create disturbances in the South China Sea", he said.
"This will only exacerbate tensions and undermine regional stability."

If faced with infringements or provocations, China will "take necessary measures to respond firmly", Chen warned, in order to "resolutely thwart any attempts to plunge the South China Sea into chaos".

The defense deal between Australia and the Philippines involves enhanced maritime activities, sharing of information and defense infrastructure development as key elements, according to Canberra.—with a report from Agence France Presse/AOL, GMA News
